entry.title: How to Simulate a SAP BTP Request to an On-Premise S/4HANA System Using Postman
entry.content:
How to Simulate a SAP BTP Request to an On-Premise S/4HANA System Using Postman

I recently ran into an issue while trying to consume data from the standard APIs exposed by an on-premise S/4HANA system through the CAP backend of a Fiori application deployed on SAP BTP and exposed via SAP Build Work Zone. The requests were failing at the Cloud Connector level, but I couldn’t find any error logs or relevant traces, either in SAP Cloud Connector or on the S/4HANA side.

To narrow down the root cause, I decided to test the API call directly from Postman, simulating a request originating from BTP so that the traffic would go through the SAP Cloud Connector. This allowed me to isolate the connectivity layer and determine whether the issue was related to the Cloud Connector configuration, the BTP configuration, the S/4HANA backend, or the CAP application itself.

I couldn’t find any end-to-end blog post or tutorial covering this specific scenario. That’s why I decided to share my experience here, along with the key steps and configuration required to get it working. The Postman collection used in the tutorial can be found on GitHub.

TL;DR

This approach did not directly identify the root cause of the error in Postman, but since the Postman request was successful, it allowed both the SAP S/4HANA system and the SAP Cloud Connector configuration to be ruled out as potential causes.

I therefore focused my investigation on the BTP side. I discovered that the destination I expected to be used at the subaccount level correctly configured and pointing to the appropriate virtual host URL of the on-premise system was actually being overridden by another destination with the same name, defined at the Cloud Foundry space level in the Destination service instance. This space-level destination contained an incorrect URL, which explained why the requests originating from the CAP application were failing.

Understanding SAP Cloud Connector

Communication between SAP S/4HANA and the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) is established through a secure tunnel provided by the SAP Cloud Connector. The Cloud Connector enables secure connectivity between on-premise systems and SAP BTP without exposing internal servers directly to the Internet.

The connection is initiated from the on-premise network, with the SAP Cloud Connector establishing an outbound TLS connection to SAP BTP. BTP therefore does not need to initiate an inbound connection to the on-premise network, eliminating the need to open inbound ports in the corporate firewall.

The SAP Cloud Connector then maps a virtual host (Virtual Host) to the corresponding internal host (Internal Host) of the SAP S/4HANA system. Applications running on SAP BTP use the virtual host when making requests to the on-premise system. The Cloud Connector transparently routes these requests to the mapped internal host through the established secure tunnel.

Understanding SAP Connectivity Service

On the SAP BTP side, the Connectivity service is responsible for managing communication with remote systems. It provides a mechanism to define objects called Destinations, which centralize the connection parameters required by applications to access target systems, such as the URL, authentication settings, proxy configuration, and other connectivity-related properties.

The Connectivity service also provides an internal HTTP proxy that is accessible only from SAP BTP runtime environments. This proxy acts as the communication layer between applications running on BTP and on-premise systems, routing requests through the SAP Cloud Connector.

This architecture keeps the connectivity endpoint isolated from the public Internet. As a result, external clients such as Postman or locally running applications cannot directly access this internal proxy endpoint. Only applications running within the appropriate SAP BTP runtime environment can use it to reach the on-premise system through the established Cloud Connector tunnel.

Request Flow

To reproduce, using Postman, the communication flow of a request sent by the CAP backend of a SAP Fiori application deployed on SAP BTP to an on-premise SAP S/4HANA system, we need to replicate the same communication path and connectivity components involved in the original request.

Step 1: Obtain an OAuth Access Token for SAP BTP Connectivity

To access the SAP BTP network proxy from outside the BTP runtime environment, Postman must first obtain an access token. This is done by sending a POST request from Postman to the UAA authentication endpoint exposed by the SAP BTP Connectivity service.

First, create an instance of the Connectivity service and generate a dedicated Service Key for this test scenario. 

The Service Key contains the credentials and endpoint information required to authenticate with the Connectivity service and obtain the OAuth access token. 

For the token request, the base authentication URL is provided in the url property of the Service Key. To obtain the OAuth access token, append the /oauth/token suffix to this URL.

The Authorization header of the token request contains the application credentials used to authenticate against SAP BTP. For this request, I use Basic Authentication, with the clientid and clientsecret values from the Service Key as the username and password, respectively. 

The request body contains the grant_type parameter set to password, along with the username and password of a user account from the BTP subaccount. This allows me to obtain an OAuth access token by authenticating on behalf of that user account. The resulting token can then be used to authenticate subsequent requests through the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy.

Send the request to obtain the JWT access token. This token acts as a credential that allows Postman to authenticate with the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy and demonstrate that it is an authorized client. Without a valid access token, the BTP Connectivity proxy will reject the request at the next step with a 407 Proxy Authentication Required response.

Step 2: Establish the SSH Network Tunnel

Before sending the request to the S/4HANA system, we need to address a second infrastructure-level challenge: the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy is exposed through a private IP address that is not directly reachable from the public Internet, where Postman is running.

To overcome this limitation, we establish an SSH tunnel (port forwarding) to a Cloud Foundry application that has access to the Connectivity service. This tunnel acts as a technical bridge, forwarding traffic from our local port (localhost:20003) directly to the private IP address and port of the BTP Connectivity proxy (X.X.X.X:20003). This allows Postman to effectively reach the BTP Connectivity proxy as if the request were originating from within the BTP environment.

Open a terminal and log in to the Cloud Foundry environment using cf api and cf login. Enable SSH access for the application and the Cloud Foundry space by running the following commands:

cf enable-ssh <APP_NAME>
cf allow-space-ssh <SPACE_NAME>
cf restage <APP_NAME>

Once SSH access has been enabled for both the application and the Cloud Foundry space, open the SSH tunnel using the following command:

ssh <app-name> -N -T -L <onpremise_proxy_http_port>:<onpremise_proxy_host>:<forwarded_local_port>

In my case, I reused local port 20003, as it was not already in use on my machine.

Step 3: Configure the Proxy and Send the Business Request to SAP S/4HANA

Once the network tunnel and access token are in place, we can configure the final request in Postman to retrieve business data from the SAP S/4HANA API_BUSINESS_PARTNER API. The request URL uses the Virtual Host and Virtual Port exposed and configured in the SAP Cloud Connector.

In Postman’s global settings, configure a Custom Proxy pointing to localhost:20003, which is the local entry point of our SSH tunnel. This configuration routes the request through the SSH tunnel to the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy, allowing Postman to leverage the BTP connectivity path to reach the on-premise SAP S/4HANA system.

In the Proxy Server configuration, enter the following values:

  • Protocol: http
  • Host: localhost
  • Port: <forwarded_local_port>

In Postman, create a new GET request to retrieve data from the on-premise SAP S/4HANA system. The request URL is composed of the following elements:

  • The Virtual Host of the SAP S/4HANA system exposed through the SAP Cloud Connector.
  • The Business Partner OData service URI: /sap/opu/odata/SAP/API_BUSINESS_PARTNER/A_BusinessPartner
  • The query parameters used to specify the SAP client and limit the number of Business Partners returned: ?sap-client=<client>&$top=10. In this example, $top=10 limits the response to the first 10 Business Partners.

In the Authorization tab, configure Basic Auth and provide the SAP S/4HANA system credentials (Username / Password) required to access the API.

The SAP BTP Connectivity proxy and the SAP Cloud Connector essentially act as a secure communication layer for routing the request. Once the request reaches the SAP S/4HANA system, it still needs to be authenticated and authorized by the SAP Gateway.

The Basic Authentication credentials provided in the request are therefore used by SAP S/4HANA to authenticate the caller and determine whether the user has the required authorizations to access or modify the requested business data.

To authenticate the request against the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy, we manually add the Proxy-Authorization header in Postman’s Headers tab. There is a technical detail worth mentioning here: Postman handles the Proxy-Authorization header, but this particular scenario requires a non-standard Basic Authentication format where the username is the JWT access token and the password is empty. Therefore, we need to Base64-encode the following string: "<token_jwt>:". The trailing colon (:) is important because it separates the username from the empty password. The resulting value is then sent in the following format:

Proxy-Authorization: Basic <Base64_encoded_value>

This allows the BTP Connectivity proxy to extract the JWT from the Basic Authentication credentials and validate the request before forwarding it through the Connectivity path. To automate this step, I use an After Response script in the first request to retrieve the token_jwt and encode it in Base64. This allows the Proxy-Authorization header to be generated dynamically from the access token  : 

const jsonData = pm.response.json();
pm.test("Status code is 200", function () {
    pm.response.to.have.status(200);
});

pm.test("Access token is present", function () {
    pm.expect(jsonData.access_token).to.be.a('string');
    pm.collectionVariables.set("access_token", jsonData.access_token);
});

const token = pm.collectionVariables.get("access_token");
const rawString = token + ":";
const base64Encoded = "Basic " + btoa(rawString);
pm.collectionVariables.set("base64EncodedToken", base64Encoded);

If you use a Location ID to identify your SAP Cloud Connector instance, you must also include it in the request headers using the SAP-Connectivity-SCC-Location_ID header.

Request Flow

When clicking Send in Postman, the request follows the complete connectivity path:

  1. Postman sends the request through the local SSH tunnel.
  2. The request reaches the Cloud Foundry application running on SAP BTP.
  3. The request is authenticated by the SAP BTP Connectivity proxy using the JWT access token.
  4. The Connectivity proxy routes the request through the SAP Cloud Connector tunnel.
  5. The request reaches the on-premise SAP S/4HANA system.
  6. SAP S/4HANA authenticates the request using the configured Basic Authentication credentials and executes the requested operation.

This reproduces, from Postman, the same connectivity path used by the CAP backend of the Fiori application to communicate with the on-premise SAP S/4HANA system.

Don’t forget to close the SSH tunnel and disable SSH access on the Cloud Foundry application and space once testing is complete.

Conclusion

Using Postman as a troubleshooting tool allowed me to isolate the issue and rule out both the SAP S/4HANA system and the SAP Cloud Connector configuration as potential root causes. Since the request successfully reached S/4HANA and returned the expected data, I was able to focus my investigation on the SAP BTP side.

I discovered that the destination configured at the subaccount level was correctly pointing to the Virtual Host of the on-premise SAP S/4HANA system. However, a destination with the same name was also defined at the Cloud Foundry space level through the Destination service instance. This second destination contained an incorrect URL. When destinations with the same name exist both at the subaccount level and in a Destination service instance bound to the application, the instance-level destination takes precedence during destination resolution. As a result, the application was using the incorrect Virtual Host URL from the Destination service instance instead of the correctly configured subaccount-level destination. This also explained why no corresponding requests or errors were visible on the SAP Cloud Connector side: the request was never reaching the Cloud Connector in the first place.

Although this is a fairly specific troubleshooting scenario, I hope this walkthrough can help you diagnose similar connectivity issues between SAP BTP and on-premise SAP S/4HANA systems. If you know of any other approaches, simpler troubleshooting techniques, or alternative ways to achieve the same result, feel free to share them in the comments. I’d be happy to hear about your experience and learn from other approaches.

Thanks for reading!

entry.title: Más allá de ABAP: Construyendo aplicaciones SAP HANA con Python, REST y Fiori
entry.content:
¿Qué sucede cuando tenemos datos en SAP HANA, pero la aplicación que necesitamos no requiere toda la arquitectura tradicional de una aplicación transaccional SAP?

Imaginemos un dashboard gerencial que necesita mostrar:

• Ventas por mes
• Utilidad por producto
• Ingresos por cliente
• KPIs
• Filtros interactivos
• Tablas analíticas
• Gráficos

La aplicación es de solo lectura.

No crea órdenes de venta, no modifica clientes ni ejecuta procesos empresariales complejos.

Entonces surge una pregunta interesante:

¿Necesitamos necesariamente construir toda la aplicación utilizando ABAP, CDS y OData?

Existe otra posibilidad arquitectónica.

El enfoque tradicional

Una arquitectura SAP común puede representarse como:

SAP HANA → ABAP/CDS → OData → SAPUI5/Fiori

ABAP proporciona la lógica de aplicación, mientras que CDS puede proporcionar modelos de datos y capacidades semánticas. OData permite exponer servicios que posteriormente pueden ser consumidos por la interfaz SAPUI5/Fiori.

Esta arquitectura es especialmente útil cuando la aplicación necesita una integración profunda con procesos empresariales SAP, lógica transaccional, autorizaciones y otras capacidades propias del ecosistema SAP.

Pero pensemos en una aplicación especializada de analítica.

Su necesidad principal podría ser simplemente:

Obtener datos de HANA → procesarlos → exponerlos → visualizarlos.

Una arquitectura diferente







































Para este tipo de escenario podemos introducir una API REST entre HANA y la interfaz Fiori:

SAP HANA → Python/FastAPI → REST/JSON → SAPUI5/Fiori

La API se conecta directamente a SAP HANA mediante un driver de base de datos.

Ejecuta consultas SQL y agregaciones analíticas y expone endpoints REST específicos, por ejemplo:

GET /sales
GET /sales/summary
GET /sales/timeseries
GET /sales/by-product
GET /sales/by-client

La respuesta es JSON.

SAPUI5 consume ese JSON mediante su modelo de datos y lo transforma en la experiencia de usuario:

REST/JSON → Modelo SAPUI5 → Tablas + Gráficos + KPIs + Filtros

La separación es bastante clara:

HANA proporciona los datos.

Python proporciona el servicio de aplicación.

REST proporciona la interfaz.

Fiori proporciona la experiencia de usuario.

Entonces, ¿esto reemplaza ABAP/CDS?

No necesariamente.

La pregunta importante no debería ser:

“¿Es Python mejor que ABAP?”

La pregunta debería ser:

“¿Qué arquitectura se adapta mejor a los requisitos de la aplicación?”

Para una aplicación profundamente integrada con procesos empresariales SAP, la arquitectura tradicional ABAP/CDS/OData puede proporcionar capacidades que una API REST sencilla no pretende reemplazar.

Para una aplicación analítica especializada y de solo lectura, una API REST puede proporcionar una separación clara entre la base de datos, la capa de servicios y el frontend.

Podemos visualizar ambas arquitecturas así:

Enfoque tradicional Enfoque desacoplado

SAP HANASAP HANA
ABAP / CDSPython / FastAPI
ODataREST / JSON
SAPUI5 / FioriSAPUI5 / Fiori
Orientado a procesos SAPOrientado a aplicaciones especializadas

¿Dónde entra Docker?

La API y el frontend también pueden empaquetarse y desplegarse de manera independiente mediante contenedores.

La arquitectura puede quedar así:

SAP HANA

↓

Python / FastAPI

↓

REST / JSON

↓

SAPUI5 / Fiori

↓

Tablas • Gráficos • KPIs • Filtros

Cada capa tiene una responsabilidad claramente definida.

Y aquí está quizás la parte más interesante de esta arquitectura.

No tenemos que pensar en SAP HANA y el desarrollo moderno de aplicaciones como mundos separados.

Podemos mantener SAP HANA como plataforma de datos empresarial y utilizar una capa de servicios independiente para construir aplicaciones especializadas alrededor de HANA.

El resultado no es un reemplazo del desarrollo tradicional de SAP.

Es otra opción arquitectónica.

Más allá de ABAP significa plantear una pregunta diferente:

¿Cuál es la arquitectura más adecuada para los requisitos de nuestra aplicación, aprovechando al mismo tiempo SAP HANA y Fiori?

En algunos casos, la respuesta será:

SAP HANA → ABAP/CDS → OData → Fiori

En otros, especialmente para una aplicación analítica y de solo lectura, podría ser:

SAP HANA → Python → REST → Fiori

entry.title: Beyond ABAP: Building SAP HANA Applications with Python, REST, and Fiori
entry.content:
What if you have SAP HANA data, but the application you need doesn't require a traditional transactional SAP application stack?

Imagine a management dashboard that needs to show:

• Sales by month
• Profit by product
• Revenue by customer
• KPIs
• Interactive filters
• Analytical tables
• Charts

The application is read-only. It doesn't create sales orders, modify business partners, or execute complex SAP business processes.

Do we necessarily need to build the entire application using the traditional ABAP/CDS/OData approach?

There is another architectural possibility.

The traditional approach

A common SAP architecture looks like:

SAP HANA → ABAP/CDS → OData → SAPUI5/Fiori

ABAP provides application logic, while CDS can provide data models and analytical semantics. OData exposes services that can then be consumed by the UI.

This architecture is particularly useful when the application needs deep integration with SAP business processes, transactional behavior, authorization concepts, and enterprise application logic.

But consider a specialized analytics application.

Its primary requirement may simply be:

Get data from HANA → process it → expose it → visualize it.

A different architecture

For this type of scenario, we can introduce a REST API between HANA and the Fiori frontend:

SAP HANA → Python/FastAPI → REST/JSON → SAPUI5/Fiori

The API connects directly to SAP HANA using a database driver.







































It executes SQL queries and analytical aggregations and exposes focused REST endpoints such as:

GET /sales
GET /sales/summary
GET /sales/timeseries
GET /sales/by-product
GET /sales/by-client

The response is JSON.

SAPUI5 consumes the JSON through its model layer and transforms the data into the user experience:

REST/JSON → SAPUI5 Model → Tables + Charts + KPIs + Filters

The separation is straightforward:

HANA provides the data.

Python provides the application service.

REST provides the interface.

Fiori provides the user experience.

So, is this a replacement for ABAP/CDS?

Not necessarily.

The important question is not:

"Is Python better than ABAP?"

It is:

"What architecture fits the application?"

For an application deeply integrated with SAP business processes, the traditional ABAP/CDS/OData architecture can provide capabilities that a simple REST service does not attempt to replace.

For a specialized read-only analytics application, however, a REST API can provide a relatively simple separation between the database, service layer, and frontend.

The two architectures can therefore be viewed as alternatives for different scenarios:

Traditional Decoupled

HANAHANA
ABAP / CDSPython / FastAPI
ODataREST / JSON
SAPUI5 / FioriSAPUI5 / Fiori
Business-process orientedSpecialized application oriented

Where does Docker fit?

The API and frontend can also be packaged independently as containers.

That gives us:

SAP HANA

↓

Python/FastAPI

↓

REST/JSON

↓

SAPUI5/Fiori

↓

Tables • Charts • KPIs • Filters

Each layer has a clearly defined responsibility.

And that is perhaps the most interesting part of this architecture.

We don't have to think of SAP HANA and modern application development as mutually exclusive worlds.

We can keep SAP HANA as the enterprise data platform and use a separate service layer to build specialized applications around it.

The result is not a replacement for traditional SAP development.

It is another architectural option.

Beyond ABAP means asking a different question:

What is the simplest architecture that satisfies the requirements of the application while still taking advantage of SAP HANA and Fiori?

Sometimes the answer will be ABAP/CDS/OData.

Sometimes, for a focused read-only application, the answer might be:

SAP HANA → Python → REST → Fiori.

entry.title: Booking an Ocean LCL Shipment in SAP TM
entry.content:
Most people who haven't worked inside a freight forwarder's operations team assume international shipping is simple put goods in a box, put the box on a ship, and the box arrives. It isn't. Between the moment a customer asks for a quote and the moment a container leaves port, SAP TM is quietly stitching together a dozen small decisions carrier, schedule, container type, consolidation partners, empty equipment, customs attributes. Get any one of them wrong and the shipment either sits at the gateway, or the invoice comes out wrong three weeks later.

The Forwarding Order
Every international shipment in SAP TM begins life as a forwarding order. A customer the shipper comes to the LSP with cargo that needs to move from A to B, and the forwarding order is where that request gets captured who the shipper and consignee are, where the goods are picked up and delivered, what the cargo looks like, and which incoterm governs who pays for what.
The forwarding order type controls more than it looks like it should. It decides whether a freight unit gets built automatically, whether charges get calculated on save, whether the shipment gets tracked through SAP Event Management, and what tabs even show up on the screen. Pick the wrong order type and you'll spend the rest of the process fighting the system instead of using it.
I've seen that go wrong in a very concrete way. On a legacy batch of forwarding orders during a freight settlement stabilization effort, a handful of orders had been created against an order type that didn't have automatic freight unit building switched on. Nobody noticed until settlement, because the charges still calculated just against the wrong cargo picture. Tracing it back meant going order type by order type through Customizing, because the settlement document itself only showed a total, not which upstream setting had produced it.


Customizing "Automatic Freight Unit Building on Save" left unchecked on a copied order type:


Forwarding Order creation screen looks like once the shipper, consignee, and order type are filled in:

General data, the incoterm, and the business partner table. But that partner table matters more than it looks. In an LCL scenario, the shipper on this order is rarely the only cargo owner going into that container. A forwarding order is just one customer's slice of a much bigger consolidated shipment, and the system needs to know exactly whose freight this is before it can even think about combining it with anyone else's.

Document Flow
SAP TM's international shipment process isn't one document it's a chain: quotation, forwarding order, freight unit, freight order or freight booking, and eventually a settlement document that feeds accounting. The course material lays this out cleanly:

                International Outbound Transportation

Goods get packed at the shipper's warehouse, containers move to the port of loading under drop-off carriage, the ocean carrier handles main carriage under an FOB term (meaning the LSP had to pre-book freight capacity before any of this happened), and then final delivery gets arranged out of the port of discharge to the consignee. Every one of those handoffs is a separate planning segment in SAP TM, and every segment has its own timing that has to be worked backward from the vessel's actual sailing date.

SAP TM ships with sea as the default main-carriage mode, but a real export rarely uses just one mode of transport. The main carriage the ocean leg is planned first because it's the most constrained and complex piece, and the truck or rail legs on either end get scheduled around it, not the other way around.

 Hierarchy: Vehicle resource, Means of transport and Transportation mode

The means of transport is the piece that trips people up. It's not the ship itself it's the category of vehicle resource (a specific container vessel, for instance) linked into the transportation network, connected to lanes and geography, and optionally flagged as "scheduled" if it runs on a fixed weekly departure. That scheduled flag is what makes gateway schedules possible in the first place.

Before Booking Capacity
Freight forwarding in an FOB / prebooked scenario, you often reserve space on a vessel before you know exactly what's going into it. That's what freight booking is for. It's the reservation general data, the carrier, the transportation stages, cargo capacity, even carrier ranking for sea freight and it exists independently of any one customer's forwarding order.

Once that booking is confirmed, it looks like this

Notice the capacity line at the top right “42 of 60 TEU used." That single field is the reason LCL consolidation works at all. A booking has a hard TEU ceiling tied to the equipment on board, and every forwarding order that gets assigned to it eats into that number. The planner's real job is packing that number as close to full as possible without going over, across cargo that belongs to completely unrelated customers.

Gateway Schedules: The Timetable Behind the Booking
A freight booking has to sit on top of an actual sailing, and that's where gateway schedules come in. A gateway schedule connects two container freight stations (CFS) one at origin, one at destination and it can pull its departure rules and voyage numbers straight from a carrier's published schedule, so planners aren't manually typing vessel names every week.
That link between the network and the actual sailing is more fragile than it looks. I saw it break for real during the 2017 Gulf blockade while I was on the SAP TM implementation at GWC Logistics in Qatar: gateway schedules had been built around routes that simply stopped existing overnight. Vessels that used to call at neighboring regional ports couldn't anymore, and for weeks, CFS assignments had to be overridden shipment by shipment while the transportation network catalog caught up. It was a good lesson in how much of "the schedule" is really just an assumption that the network stays open.

Sailing schedule concept

In the system, that concept becomes a plain list a planner actually works from  which sailing has room, which is nearly full, and when the next one leaves:

This is the screen a booking planner lives in during peak season. "Near Full" on a sailing means exactly one thing operationally if two more customers' cargo needs to go out this week, one of them is waiting for the next vessel.

Consolidation of LCL
A forwarding order in an LCL scenario is one customer's partial load. The freight forwarder's actual value add is consolidating multiple customers' forwarding orders into shared containers, based on weight and volume that each order has already captured. That consolidation can happen manually, from a schedule, from the transportation cockpit, or by copying a prior booking but the goal is always the same fill the container without exceeding it, using cargo from customers who have no idea the others exist.

Shipping container types

Equipment type matters here beyond just "big box" versus "small box." Reefers, open-tops, flat racks, and standard dry containers all have different tare weights and capacity limits, and the system calculates TEU and tare weight automatically once the equipment group and type are entered on the forwarding order. Get the equipment type wrong and the capacity math on the whole booking goes sideways which is exactly the kind of mismatch that surfaced in that settlement stabilization work: one wrong equipment type on a small number of orders, and TEU utilization across an entire booking stopped adding up, with nothing on the settlement side flagging it as an equipment issue rather than a cost issue.

Empty Containers Are a Business Process, Not an Afterthought
LSPs frequently have to provide empty containers to a customer, separate from actually shipping their goods and sometimes the customer wants the LSP to also collect and return those empties afterward. SAP TM handles this as an explicit field level decision on the forwarding order item, not a workaround "Empty Provisioning" and "Empty Return" flags on the cargo item tell the system whether to generate a completely separate freight unit and transportation unit just for moving empty equipment around, independent of the loaded shipment.
It's a small feature, but it's the difference between a container repositioning cost that's tracked properly and one that just gets absorbed as an unexplained variance later.

Air Freight 
Air LCL works almost identically, with unit load devices standing in for containers and gateways standing in for airline delivery addresses. The one real difference is the AWB type attribute. Because some countries don't allow consolidation at all, SAP TM lets you lock a forwarding order into back to back, direct shipment, or internal co-load handling and once that attribute is set (either in Customizing or directly on the document), it flows through to the air freight booking as read only. You don't get to quietly consolidate a shipment that was legally required to travel alone.

The Takeaway
Cut out the transaction codes and the acronyms, and this whole thing really just comes down to four questions the system keeps asking whose cargo is this, what's it going on, is there space left, and who's paying for which part of the trip. The forwarding order handles the first one. The freight booking and gateway schedule cover the next two. The incoterm on the forwarding order takes care of the fourth. Everything else equipment types, empty provisioning, Air Waybill attributes is just the system's way of dealing with the exceptions.

entry.title: Implementing Internationalization in SAP CAP: Multi-Language Support Using i18n Properties
entry.content:
Introduction

Enterprise applications rarely serve users from a single country. A Fiori app built in Bengaluru may well be used by someone in Paris or Frankfurt, and showing them English column headers everywhere isn't a great experience.

Internationalization (i18n) solves this. Instead of hardcoding texts such as Name, City, or General Information directly in CDS annotations, we externalize them into language-specific properties files. At runtime, the application loads the appropriate language-specific texts, allowing the UI to change languages without modifying the underlying application logic.

In this blog, I'll build a small CAP application with a Fiori Elements UI and demonstrate English and French translations using i18n properties files. The same approach can be extended to additional languages such as German, Hindi, and Kannada.

What actually gets translated

One thing confused me when I first set this up, so let me get it out of the way early: there are two separate i18n layers in a CAP + Fiori Elements project, and they sit in different folders.

The first is the CAP layer, a folder named _i18n at the project root. This is what translates the labels in your CDS annotations: field labels, facet headers, that kind of thing. The CAP layer is responsible for resolving i18n keys used in CDS annotations, such as field labels and facet titles, before the corresponding OData metadata is consumed by the Fiori Elements application.

The second is the UI5 layer, the i18n folder inside webapp. This handles the app title, description, and any texts you reference directly from your UI5 views or controllers. It's resolved in the browser by the standard UI5 resource model.

So when your List Report shows Nom instead of Name, that swap happened on the CAP server. The app title in the launchpad tile, on the other hand, gets translated by UI5. You need both working correctly for a fully translated app, and it's easy to spend an hour debugging the wrong one.

Neither layer touches the actual business data, by the way. If a row in your database says Bangalore, it stays Bangalore no matter what language the UI is in. Translating the data itself is a different CAP feature (localized data, using .texts entities) and isn't something I'm getting into here.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js installed
  • `@sap/cds-dk` installed globally
  • VS Code or SAP Business Application Studio
  • Basic familiarity with CAP and Fiori Elements

Step 1: Define the data model

Create db/schema.cds with a simple students entity:

namespace db;

entity students {
    key id   : String;
        name : String;
        age  : Integer;
        city : String;
}

Nothing fancy. Four fields is enough to demonstrate the translation part, which is really what this post is about.

Step 2: Expose it as a service

Create srv/service.cds:

using { db.students } from '../db/schema';

service MyService {
    entity entity1 as projection on students;
}

This gives us an OData V4 service at /odata/v4/my/ with a single entity set.

Step 3: Add sample data

CAP can generate CSV sample files for you:

cds add data --records 10

This creates db/data/db-students.csv. I replaced the generated values with something more readable:

id,name,age,city
S001,Chetan,25,Gadag
S002,Rahul,24,Bangalore
S003,Akash,26,Mysore
S004,Priya,23,Hubli
S005,Anil,25,Dharwad

Then add SQLite as the local database and deploy:

npm add @cap-js/sqlite
cds deploy

Step 4: Generate the Fiori Elements app

Use the Fiori generator (`@sap/generator-fiori`) to create a List Report Object Page application on top of MyService. Once that's done, the project structure looks like this:

internationalization/
│
├── _i18n/                          <-- CAP layer: translates CDS annotations
│   ├── i18n.properties
│   ├── i18n_en.properties
│   ├── i18n_de.properties
│   ├── i18n_fr.properties
│   ├── i18n_hi.properties
│   └── i18n_kn.properties
│
├── app/
│   └── project1/
│       ├── webapp/
│       │   └── i18n/               <-- UI5 layer: app title, description
│       │       └── i18n.properties
│       ├── annotations.cds
│       ├── manifest.json
│       └── ...
│
├── db/
│   ├── data/
│   │   └── db-students.csv
│   └── schema.cds
│
├── srv/
│   └── service.cds
│
├── package.json
└── README.md

The _i18n folder at the project root is the recommended location for CAP text bundles. It allows the translations to be shared across the CAP project.

Step 5: Create the i18n properties files

This is where the actual translation lives. Create an _i18n folder at the project root and add the default file i18n.properties:

appTitle=Students Application
appDescription=Student information
uid=ID
name=Name
age=Age
city=City
generalInformation=General Information

Then create i18n_fr.properties with the same keys and French values:

appTitle=Application des étudiants
appDescription=Informations sur les étudiants
uid=ID
name=Nom
age=Âge
city=Ville
generalInformation=Informations générales

Every other language follows the exact same pattern: same keys, different values. I added i18n_en, i18n_de, i18n_hi, and i18n_kn alongside the French one, but since they're just repeats of the structure above with translated strings, I won't paste all of them here.

A few things worth keeping in mind while you do this. The naming convention is i18n_<locale>.properties: _fr for French, _de for German, _kn for Kannada. The plain i18n.properties, with no suffix, acts as the fallback. If a user's browser is set to a language you haven't translated, or a key is missing from their file, CAP quietly falls back to this one. And there's no compile-time check tying your annotation keys to your properties file keys, so if you get a key name wrong you won't see an error, you'll just see the literal key name rendered in the UI.

The UI5 side gets its own, much smaller file at app/project1/webapp/i18n/i18n.properties, holding just appTitle and appDescription. Keeping the two sets of files apart isn't an accident. The CAP files are read by the server, the UI5 file by the browser, and they're resolved through completely different code paths.

Step 6: Use the keys in annotations

Open app/project1/annotations.cds and replace the hardcoded labels with i18n references using the {i18n>key} syntax:

using MyService as service from '../../srv/service';

annotate service.entity1 with @(
    UI.FieldGroup #GeneratedGroup : {
        $Type : 'UI.FieldGroupType',
        Data  : [
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>uid}',  Value : id   },
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>name}', Value : name },
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>age}',  Value : age  },
            { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>city}', Value : city }
        ]
    },
    UI.Facets : [
        {
            $Type  : 'UI.ReferenceFacet',
            ID     : 'GeneratedFacet1',
            Label  : '{i18n>generalInformation}',
            Target : '@UI.FieldGroup#GeneratedGroup'
        }
    ],
    UI.LineItem : [
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>uid}',  Value : id   },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>name}', Value : name },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>age}',  Value : age  },
        { $Type : 'UI.DataField', Label : '{i18n>city}', Value : city }
    ]
);

I also changed the facet label from the hardcoded 'General Information' to '{i18n>generalInformation}'. It's easy to translate the column headers and forget the section titles, but users notice those just as much.

These keys are resolved against the root _i18n folder, nothing in webapp. When a request comes in, CAP checks the locale, picks the matching properties file, and returns a $metadata document with the labels already translated. You can actually see this happen by opening /odata/v4/my/$metadata?sap-language=fr directly in the browser. The French labels are sitting right there in the EDMX, before UI5 has done anything at all.

Step 7: Wire i18n into manifest.json

This part is purely UI5 territory. It has nothing to do with the annotation labels from the last step. The Fiori generator sets most of it up for you, but it's worth knowing what's actually happening.

sap.app points to the webapp bundle and uses double braces for the title and description:

"sap.app": {
    "id": "project1",
    "type": "application",
    "i18n": "i18n/i18n.properties",
    "title": "{{appTitle}}",
    "description": "{{appDescription}}"
}

Note the syntax difference: {{key}} here in the descriptor, versus {i18n>key} everywhere else.

Under sap.ui5, two resource models get declared:

"models": {
    "i18n": {
        "type": "sap.ui.model.resource.ResourceModel",
        "settings": {
            "bundleName": "project1.i18n.i18n"
        }
    },
    "@i18n": {
        "type": "sap.ui.model.resource.ResourceModel",
        "uri": "i18n/i18n.properties"
    }
}

Both models belong to the UI5 application layer and point to the application's webapp/i18n/i18n.properties bundle. They are separate from the CAP _i18n bundle used to resolve texts referenced from CDS annotations. The CDS annotation labels are resolved by CAP before the Fiori Elements application consumes the corresponding metadata.

Step 8: Run and test

Start the application:

npm run start

The app comes up in English first, since that's the default:


Now switch the language. In Chrome, go to Settings → Languages, add French, and move it to the top of the list. Refresh the page.

The column headers now read Nom, Âge, and Ville, and the app title has switched to Application des étudiants. The data hasn't moved, Bangalore is still Bangalore, which is what you'd expect since this whole exercise was about translating labels, not data.

If you don't want to keep flipping your browser's language setting back and forth while testing, append ?sap-language=fr to the URL instead. It overrides the detected locale for that one session and is a lot faster during development.

Conclusion

In this blog, we saw how to add internationalization to an SAP CAP and Fiori Elements application using i18n properties files. By externalizing static UI texts and referencing them through i18n keys, the same application can display labels and titles in different languages without changing the underlying application logic.

The approach keeps translations separate from the application code, making it easier to maintain and extend the application with additional languages in the future.

With this setup in place, we can provide a more localized and user-friendly Fiori experience while keeping the business data unchanged.
